intro: The Analects is a book of short sayings. Some are one sentence long. That makes them easy to quote and easy to misread. In this unit you slow down. You read famous passages from books 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 13 and 15 in James Legge's 1893 translation, word for word.

You will ask the questions close readers ask. Who is speaking, the Master or a disciple? Who is he speaking to? What English word did Legge choose, and what other words could fit? What do the nearby sayings add? How have Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Western readers taken the same line?

By the end you will be able to cite the Analects by book and chapter, explain key terms such as ren, li, xiao, de, shu and junzi, and write about a passage by describing what it says and how its readers have understood it.
bigQuestion: What does it take to read a short saying from the Analects carefully and fairly?

story.title: Still Listening at Sixty
story.kicker: A student reads Analects 2.4 aloud, and her grandfather finds his own age in it.
paragraphs: Mei has homework for her tenth-grade English class. She has to read one short passage aloud to someone at home and write down what they say. She picks Analects 2.4 from James Legge's 1893 translation, because it is short and it has numbers in it.

She reads it at the kitchen table. "At fifteen, I had my mind bent on learning. At thirty, I stood firm. At forty, I had no doubts. At fifty, I knew the decrees of Heaven." Her grandfather is peeling an orange. He stops when she reaches the line about sixty.

"At sixty, my ear was an obedient organ for the reception of truth," Mei reads. Her grandfather laughs. He says he is sixty-one, so he must be at the listening stage. He says his own teacher in Taipei made the class learn this passage by heart, and he still hears it differently every ten years.

Mei writes that down. Then she notices something. The passage is in the first person. It is Confucius describing his own life, not giving a rule for everyone. Her grandfather says some readers treat it as a map for every life, and others read it as one man's memory. Mei is not sure which reading fits better.
story.think: Is Analects 2.4 a rule for every life, or one man's account of his own? What words in the passage help you decide?

lessons.title: The First Three Questions
lessons.mainIdea: Analects 1.1 opens the book with three questions about learning, friendship and staying calm when no one notices you.
reading: The Analects begins with three questions from the Master. Legge's 1893 translation gives them this way: "Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application? Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters? Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?"

Each question expects the answer yes. That is a *rhetorical question*: a question asked to make a point, not to get information. The form invites the listener to agree rather than ordering them to. Many readers think this gentle form suits a teacher talking with students.

The three questions move outward. The first is about the learner alone. The second is about friends who share the learning. The third is about the wider world, which may ignore the learner. Traditional commentators such as Zhu Xi read the order as a path from private study to public life.

The third question uses the phrase that Legge renders "a man of complete virtue." The Chinese term is *junzi*. It first meant the son of a ruler, a noble by birth. The Analects uses it for a person noble in character. Legge usually translates it as "the superior man."

words.d: a question asked to make a point, where the expected answer is already clear
in the Analects, a person of noble character; Legge often writes "the superior man"
keeping on with a task over a long time

lessons.title: Who Is Speaking?
lessons.mainIdea: Not every saying in the Analects is from Confucius; some, like 1.2, come from his disciples.
reading: Analects 1.1 begins "The Master said." Analects 1.2 does not. It begins with the words of Yu Zi, a disciple. Legge gives his name in the older spelling of his day. Close readers always check the opening line of a saying, because it tells you who is talking.

The Analects is a *compilation*: a book gathered from many sources by later hands. Most scholars think disciples and their own students collected the sayings over several generations after Confucius died, around 479 BCE by the traditional date. Some books may be later than others. Scholars still debate the order and the dates.

Because of this, a *disciple* can speak with real weight in the book. Yu Zi and Zeng Zi are even called "Zi," "master," a sign of respect. Some scholars read that title as a clue that their own followers helped shape the collection. So when you cite a line, name the speaker, not just "Confucius."

words.d: a book made by gathering many pieces, often by several people over time
a student who follows a teacher and passes on the teacher's ideas
the title the Analects uses for Confucius when he speaks

check.q: Who speaks in Analects 1.2?
check.why: Analects 1.2 opens with the words of the disciple Yu Zi, not "The Master said."

check.q: What do most scholars think about how the Analects was made?

lessons.title: Counting Books and Chapters
lessons.mainIdea: Analects 2.4 means book 2, chapter 4, but some editions divide the chapters in slightly different places.
reading: The Analects has 20 books. Each book holds short numbered chapters. A citation like 2.4 means book 2, chapter 4. Legge uses this book.chapter system, and most English translations follow it. That is why a reader can find the same passage in almost any edition.

The numbers are not perfect. Editors have sometimes split one saying into two chapters, or joined two into one. So book 10, for example, is numbered differently in some translations. A saying can be one number off. Careful writers name the translation they used, so a reader can find the same line.

The chapter numbers are not in the oldest texts. The early Chinese text was written as a stream of sayings. Later editors and commentators marked where each saying began. The numbering is a tool for readers. It is not part of what the disciples first wrote down.

words.d: a note that tells readers exactly where a quotation comes from
one particular published version of a text
the way the Analects is cited, as in 15.23 for book 15, chapter 23

lessons.title: Reading Legge Today
lessons.mainIdea: Legge's 1893 English is old and sometimes wordy, but it is exact enough to quote and is free for anyone to use.
reading: James Legge was a Scottish missionary and scholar who spent many years in Hong Kong. He worked with Chinese scholars, including Wang Tao, on his translations. His first volume of the Analects came out in 1861, and a revised edition in 1893. Later he became the first professor of Chinese at Oxford.

Legge's English sounds old today. He writes "the superior man" for junzi and "propriety" for *li*, the rites and good manners of the tradition. He puts his own added words in brackets or italics to show what is not in the Chinese. Modern translators often choose shorter words.

Because Legge's translation is in the *public domain*, anyone may quote it freely. That is one reason this course uses it. Readers also note that Legge's Christian background sometimes shaped his word choices. Scholars compare him with later translators to see where his readings are his own.

words.d: ritual and proper conduct; the rites and manners of the Confucian tradition; Legge often writes "propriety"

lessons.title: Filial Piety as the Root
lessons.mainIdea: In Analects 1.2 the disciple Yu Zi calls filial piety and respect for elder brothers the root of goodness.
reading: Analects 1.2 closes with a question from Yu Zi. Legge translates it: "Filial piety and fraternal submission!—are they not the root of all benevolent actions?" The saying uses a picture from farming. A plant grows from its root. Yu Zi suggests that goodness grows from how a person acts at home.

*Xiao* is the Chinese word Legge renders "filial piety." It means respect and care for one's parents and ancestors. "Fraternal submission" is respect for older brothers. The word "benevolent" translates *ren*, the Analects' word for full human goodness.

Readers have taken this saying in different ways. Many Confucian teachers read it as the order of learning: first home, then the wider world. Some modern critics worry that it puts family loyalty above fairness to strangers. Others answer that the root is where goodness starts, not where it ends.

words.d: filial piety; respect and care for one's parents and ancestors
full human goodness or humaneness; Legge writes "benevolence" or "perfect virtue"
having to do with brothers

lessons.title: More Than Feeding
lessons.mainIdea: In Analects 2.7 Confucius says caring for parents means reverence, not only food and shelter.
reading: A disciple named Ziyou asks about filial piety in Analects 2.7. The Master answers with a sharp comparison. In Legge's words: "The filial piety of now-a-days means the support of one's parents. But dogs and horses likewise are able to do something in the way of support;—without reverence, what is there to distinguish the one support given from the other?"

The point turns on the word *reverence*: deep respect shown in attitude and action. Food and a roof are needed. But the Master says they are not enough on their own. What makes care filial is the respect behind it. The comparison with animals is meant to make the listener stop and think.

Commentators read the dogs and horses line in two ways. One reading says people also feed their dogs and horses, so feeding parents is no special honor. Another says dogs and horses themselves serve people. Both readings reach the same end: support without reverence falls short of xiao.

words.d: deep respect shown in how one feels and acts
in 2.7, providing food and care for one's parents
a scholar who writes notes explaining a classic text

lessons.title: Filial Piety in Living Families
lessons.mainIdea: Xiao is read and practiced in many ways today, from ancestor rites to daily care, and people disagree about its limits.
reading: Many families in China, Taiwan, Korea, Vietnam and the Chinese diaspora still honor parents and ancestors in visible ways. At Qingming in spring, families visit graves and sweep them. Some families keep ancestor tablets at home and offer food or incense. Families in Illinois do these things too.

People connect these practices to xiao in different ways. For some it is a religious duty to ancestors. For others it is family memory and respect. Whether Confucian ancestor rites are religious is itself debated by scholars and by the families who keep them. This course names the views and does not settle it.

Modern readers also debate xiao's limits. Some ask how it fits with a young person's own choices. Some point out that tradition asked more of daughters-in-law than of sons. Others defend xiao as a strong bond across generations. Close reading helps: 2.7 asks for reverence, not blind obedience.

words.d: a spring festival when many families visit and sweep their ancestors' graves
a wooden plaque with an ancestor's name, kept at home or in a hall and honored
a people living far from their homeland

lessons.title: The North Polar Star
lessons.mainIdea: Analects 2.1 compares a ruler who governs by virtue to the pole star, which stays still while all stars turn toward it.
reading: Analects 2.1 is one sentence long. Legge translates: "He who exercises government by means of his virtue may be compared to the north polar star, which keeps its place and all the stars turn towards it." The image is taken from the night sky. The pole star seems to stay fixed while the others circle around it.

"Virtue" here translates *de*. In early Chinese, de meant a kind of moral power or pull. A person of de draws others without force. So the ruler in 2.1 does not chase the people. The people turn to him, the way the stars seem to turn around the pole.

An *analogy* compares two things to explain one of them. Analects 2.1 uses an analogy from astronomy to explain government. Readers ask where the analogy stops. Stars have no choice. People do. Some commentators say that is the point: good rule works like a natural pull, not a command.

words.d: virtue or moral power; the pull a good person has on others
a comparison that explains one thing by pointing to another like it
the star near the north celestial pole that seems to stay still while others circle it

lessons.title: Shame, Not Just Punishment
lessons.mainIdea: Analects 2.3 says laws and punishments make people avoid penalties, but virtue and ritual give them a sense of shame and make them good.
reading: Analects 2.3 sets two kinds of government side by side. Legge: "If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame. If they be led by virtue, and uniformity sought to be given them by the rules of propriety, they will have the sense of shame, and moreover will become good."

The saying is built as a *parallel*: two sentences with the same shape and different content. Laws are paired with punishments. Virtue is paired with propriety, or li. The results differ too. The first gives people a way to escape penalties. The second changes what they feel inside.

Later thinkers argued with this idea. The Legalist writers, such as Han Feizi, held that clear laws and firm rewards and punishments keep order. Confucian readers answered with 2.3. Many modern readers see a middle ground, with both laws and shared values. The Analects' own position is clear: virtue and li work deeper.

words.d: two lines built with the same shape so a reader compares them
a school of early Chinese thought that stressed strict laws, rewards and punishments
in 2.3, an inner sense of what is wrong that makes a person hold back

lessons.title: A Life in Stages
lessons.mainIdea: In Analects 2.4 Confucius describes his own life in six stages, from setting his mind on learning at fifteen to following his heart at seventy.
reading: Analects 2.4 is one of the best-known passages in the book. Legge's version ends: "At sixty, my ear was an obedient organ for the reception of truth. At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired, without transgressing what was right." It is spoken in the first person, as the Master's own story.

The stages move from effort to ease. At fifteen the Master sets his mind on learning. At thirty he stands firm. At fifty he knows the decrees of Heaven, *Tian*, the high power that early Chinese thought linked to order and fate. At seventy, what he wants and what is right no longer pull apart.

Readers use the passage in different ways. In Chinese, the ages have become common names: "standing firm" for thirty, for instance. Some readers take the passage as a model for anyone's life. Others read it as one person's *reflection*, a look back over his own growth. The text itself uses "I."

words.d: Heaven; in early Chinese thought, the high power linked to order, fate and the moral world
looking back and thinking about one's own life or actions
writing that uses "I" to tell one's own story

story.title: One Word for a Whole Life
story.kicker: A disciple asks for a single word to live by, and the Master gives him one.
paragraphs: The scene in Analects 15.23 is very short. A disciple named Zigong, a clever speaker and a successful merchant, comes to the Master with a big request. He does not want a long lesson. He wants one word.

In James Legge's 1893 translation, Zigong asks: "Is there not one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one's life?" It is a bold question. Zigong is known in the Analects for quick answers. Here he asks for the shortest answer of all.

The Master replies: "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Legge prints the key word in capital letters. The Chinese word is shu. Legge chose "reciprocity," a word about give and take between people.

Readers have returned to this exchange for more than two thousand years. Some hear a simple rule. Some notice that it tells you what not to do rather than what to do. Others ask why one word needs a whole sentence to explain it. The scene is small, but the questions it raises are large.
story.think: Why might a teacher answer a request for one word with a word and a sentence? What does the sentence add?

lessons.title: To Love All Men
lessons.mainIdea: In Analects 12.22 the Master answers a question about ren with a short reply: it is to love others.
reading: Analects 12.22 opens with a student named Fan Chi. Legge writes: "Fan Ch'ih asked about benevolence. The Master said, 'It is to love all men.'" Legge uses "benevolence" for ren. The Chinese word for "men" here, ren 人, means people in general, not only males.

*Ren* is the central virtue of the Analects. It is often translated goodness, humaneness or benevolence. The Chinese character joins the sign for a person with the sign for two. Many teachers point out this shape to suggest that ren lives between people. Scholars debate how much weight that picture can bear.

The Master gives different answers about ren to different students. To Fan Chi he says love people. To others he says other things. Many readers think he fits each answer to the person asking. So no single line defines ren. A close reader gathers several answers and compares them.

words.d: the Analects' central virtue: goodness, humaneness or benevolence
Legge's usual English for ren; kindness and good will toward others
a single written Chinese sign that stands for a word or part of a word

look.title: Fan Chi Asks About Ren
look.text: Fan Ch'ih asked about benevolence. The Master said, 'It is to love all men.'
look.cite: Confucian Analects 12.22, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1893
look.prompt: Legge wrote "all men." What English words might a translator choose today, and why?

check.q: What does the Master tell Fan Chi about ren in Analects 12.22?
choices: It is to love all people
It is to obey the ruler
It is to follow the Dao
It is to fast and pray
check.why: In Legge's 12.22 the Master says benevolence "is to love all men."

check.q: Why do many readers think the Master gives different answers about ren?
choices: He fits each answer to the student asking
check.why: The Analects shows the Master teaching each student in a way that fits them.

check.q: Which English word does Legge usually use for ren?
check.why: Legge often renders ren as benevolence; propriety is li and reciprocity is shu.

lessons.title: Returning to Ritual
lessons.mainIdea: In Analects 12.1 the Master links ren to li: subduing oneself and returning to propriety.
reading: Analects 12.1 is the first chapter of book 12, and it also answers a question about ren. This time the student is Yan Hui, the Master's favorite. Legge's reply reads: "To subdue one's self and return to propriety, is perfect virtue." Here Legge writes "perfect virtue" for ren.

The saying links ren with li, ritual and proper conduct. "Subdue one's self" means holding back one's own selfish wants. "Return to propriety" means acting in the proper forms. Yan Hui then asks for details. The Master tells him to look, listen, speak and move only in line with li.

Readers argue about how inner goodness and outer ritual fit together. Some stress that li shapes the heart over time, like practice shapes a musician. Others stress that ritual without real feeling is empty, which the Analects also says in other places. Many readers see ren and li as two sides of one way of life.

words.d: ritual and proper conduct; Legge writes "propriety"
holding back one's own wants in order to act rightly
the disciple the Analects shows the Master praising most

look.title: Yan Hui Asks About Ren
look.text: To subdue one's self and return to propriety, is perfect virtue.
look.cite: Confucian Analects 12.1, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1893
look.prompt: Compare this answer with 12.22. How is the answer to Yan Hui different from the answer to Fan Chi?

check.q: In Analects 12.1, what two actions make up "perfect virtue"?
choices: Loving all men and feeding parents
Subduing oneself and returning to propriety
check.why: Legge's 12.1: "To subdue one's self and return to propriety, is perfect virtue."

check.q: Who asks about ren in Analects 12.1?
check.why: Analects 12.1 is the Master's answer to Yan Hui.

check.q: What do many readers say about ren and li?
choices: They are opposite and cannot meet
They are two sides of one way of life
Ren is Daoist and li is Buddhist
Li replaced ren after Confucius died
check.why: Readers debate the balance, but many see inner goodness and outer ritual as working together.

lessons.title: Yan Hui's Bamboo Dish
lessons.mainIdea: Analects 6.9 praises Yan Hui for keeping his joy while living in poverty.
reading: Yan Hui was poor. Analects 6.9 describes his life. Legge: "Admirable indeed was the virtue of Hui! With a single bamboo dish of rice, a single gourd dish of drink, and living in his mean narrow lane, while others could not have endured the distress, he did not allow his joy to be affected by it." The line about Hui's virtue is repeated at the end.

The passage uses *repetition*: it opens and closes with the same line of praise. This frame tells the reader what matters most. The details in the middle, a bamboo dish and a gourd cup, make the poverty concrete. "Mean" in Legge's English means poor and humble, not unkind.

Readers ask what Yan Hui's joy came from. Many Confucian readers, including the Song dynasty scholars, took it as the joy of learning and goodness. It is not joy in being poor. The Analects also records that Yan Hui died young, and that the Master grieved deeply for him.

words.d: saying the same words again to stress them or frame a passage
in Legge's older English, poor or humble, not cruel
a good quality of character; in Legge often the Chinese de

look.title: Reading the Frame
look.text: Analects 6.9 begins and ends with "Admirable indeed was the virtue of Hui!" In the middle: one bamboo dish of rice, one gourd of drink, a narrow lane, and a joy that did not change.
look.prompt: Why frame the passage with the same line twice? What do the small details in the middle add?

check.q: What does Analects 6.9 praise Yan Hui for?
choices: Keeping his joy while living in poverty
check.why: 6.9 says others could not endure his distress, but he did not let his joy be affected.

check.q: What does "mean" mean in Legge's phrase "mean narrow lane"?
check.why: In Legge's older English, mean means poor or humble.

check.q: How did many Confucian readers explain the source of Yan Hui's joy?
choices: The joy of learning and goodness
Joy in being poor for its own sake
check.why: Many Confucian readers, including Song scholars, read it as joy in learning and the Way, not in poverty itself.

lessons.title: The Negative Golden Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Analects 15.23 states a rule of reciprocity in the negative: do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself.
reading: In Analects 15.23 Zigong asks for one word to guide a whole life. Legge's Master answers: "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Many readers call this a version of the *Golden Rule*, a rule found in many traditions about treating others as you would be treated.

The form matters. The saying tells you what not to do. Scholars call this the negative form. Other traditions state the rule in a positive form: do to others what you would want. Readers argue about the difference. Some say the negative form is more modest. Others say the two forms end up close.

Legge himself, in his notes, argued that the negative form is weaker than the positive one. Many later scholars, Chinese and Western, disagree with him. They point out that the Analects also has positive statements of the same idea, such as 6.28. The debate shows how a translator's views can travel with his translation.

words.d: a rule, found in many traditions, about treating others as you would want to be treated
a rule stated as what not to do
reciprocity or considerateness; putting oneself in another's place; Legge writes "reciprocity"

look.title: One Word for Life
look.text: Tsze-kung asked, saying, "Is there not one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one's life?" The Master said, "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others."
look.cite: Confucian Analects 15.23, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1893
look.prompt: Rewrite the rule in the positive form. Does anything change in what it asks a person to do?

check.q: What word does the Master give Zigong in Analects 15.23 (in Legge)?
check.why: Legge prints "RECIPROCITY," his English for shu.

check.q: Why do scholars call 15.23 a negative form of the Golden Rule?
choices: It was later removed from the book
It says what not to do to others
It is spoken by a critic of Confucius
check.why: "Do not do to others" states the rule as what to avoid.

check.q: What did Legge argue in his notes about the negative form?
choices: That it was copied from the Bible
That it was a Daoist rule
That it was weaker than the positive form
check.why: Legge thought the negative form weaker; many later scholars disagree.

lessons.title: The One Thread
lessons.mainIdea: In Analects 4.15 the disciple Zeng Zi explains the Master's one thread as loyalty and reciprocity.
reading: Analects 4.15 is a puzzle scene. The Master tells Zeng Zi that his teaching has one thread running through it. Zeng Zi says yes, and the Master leaves. The other disciples ask what he meant. Zeng Zi answers. Legge: "The doctrine of our master is to be true to the principles of our nature and the benevolent exercise of them to others,—this and nothing more."

Legge's long phrase stands for two short Chinese words. The first is *zhong*, usually translated loyalty or doing one's best. The second is shu, reciprocity. Legge's wording is a reading, not just a translation. He explains the two words as he understands them. Modern translations are much shorter.

Notice who explains the thread. It is Zeng Zi, not the Master. Some scholars think Zeng Zi's own followers helped shape this scene. Others take it as a faithful memory. Either way, readers link 4.15 with 15.23, where shu is named again. Reading the two together is a basic close-reading move.

words.d: loyalty, or doing one's best for others; paired with shu in Analects 4.15
the single idea the Master says runs through all his teaching in 4.15
reading one passage beside another that uses the same word or idea

look.title: Two Passages, One Word
look.text: Analects 4.15: Zeng Zi names the Master's one thread as zhong and shu. Analects 15.23: the Master names shu, "reciprocity," as the one word for life.
look.prompt: What does 15.23 add to your understanding of 4.15? What does 4.15 add to 15.23?

check.q: In Analects 4.15, who explains the Master's one thread?
check.why: The Master leaves, and Zeng Zi explains the thread to the other disciples.

check.q: Which two Chinese words stand behind Legge's long phrase in 4.15?
check.why: Zeng Zi names zhong, loyalty, and shu, reciprocity.

check.q: Why do close readers link Analects 4.15 with 15.23?
choices: Both are about the pole star
check.why: Shu appears in both, so each helps explain the other.

lessons.title: How Translators Shape a Reading
lessons.mainIdea: The English words chosen for shu, ren and junzi change how readers hear the Analects.
reading: Legge gives "reciprocity" for shu. Other translators have given "consideration," "like-hearted considerateness" or "understanding." Each choice points a reader somewhere. Reciprocity suggests a fair exchange. Consideration suggests imagining how another person feels. The Chinese character joins "like" or "as" with "heart."

Translation always involves choices. A *connotation* is the feeling or extra meaning a word carries beyond its dictionary sense. "Superior man" carries a feeling of rank. "Exemplary person" carries a feeling of example. Readers who know only English meet the Analects through these connotations.

This is why scholars compare translations. They look for places where the English adds or loses meaning. Legge's notes help, because he explains his choices. When you write about the Analects, name your translation and, where it matters, show one other version beside it.

words.d: the feeling or extra meaning a word carries beyond its plain definition
a translator's chosen way of putting a word or line into another language
reciprocity or considerateness; the character joins "as" with "heart"

look.title: Four Renderings of Shu
look.text: Legge (1893): "reciprocity." Other translators: "consideration," "like-hearted considerateness," "understanding." The Chinese character shu 恕 is built from 如, "as," over 心, "heart."
look.prompt: Which English word fits the picture of "as" plus "heart" best? Explain your choice.

check.q: What is a connotation?
choices: A footnote at the end of a book
The extra feeling or meaning a word carries
check.why: A connotation is the feeling a word carries beyond its plain meaning.

check.q: Which parts make up the character shu?
check.why: Shu joins 如, as, with 心, heart; "person" plus "two" is ren.

check.q: Why do scholars compare translations of the Analects?
choices: To find the one correct English Bible
To see where the English adds or loses meaning
To prove Legge wrote the Analects
check.why: Comparing renderings shows how word choices shape a reading.

lessons.title: Making Names Correct
lessons.mainIdea: In Analects 13.3 the Master says good government starts with making names correct, so that words match reality.
reading: In Analects 13.3 the disciple Zilu asks what the Master would do first if he were asked to govern. The Master says he would make names correct. Zilu thinks this is a strange first step. The Master explains with a chain of results. Legge: "If names be not correct, language is not in accordance with the truth of things. If language be not in accordance with the truth of things, affairs cannot be carried on to success."

This teaching is called the *rectification of names*. To rectify means to set right. The idea is that words like "ruler," "father" or "minister" should match what the person actually does. When they do not, trust breaks down. The chain in 13.3 goes on to rites, music, punishments, and finally the people.

The passage uses a *chain argument*: each step leads to the next. Readers have applied it to many things. Some use it to discuss honesty in public speech. Some scholars link it to Analects 12.11, "let the ruler be ruler," where roles and names also meet.

words.d: the Confucian teaching that words and titles should match reality
to set right or correct
an argument where each step leads to the next, ending in a result

look.title: If Names Be Not Correct
look.text: If names be not correct, language is not in accordance with the truth of things. If language be not in accordance with the truth of things, affairs cannot be carried on to success.
look.cite: Confucian Analects 13.3, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1893
look.prompt: Draw the first two links of this chain. What happens at each step when words do not match things?

check.q: In Analects 13.3, what does the Master say he would do first in government?
check.why: He answers Zilu that names must first be made correct.

check.q: What does "rectification of names" mean?
choices: Making words and titles match reality
check.why: To rectify is to set right; names should fit what things and people really are.

check.q: What kind of argument does 13.3 use?
choices: A chain argument, each step leading to the next
check.why: 13.3 moves step by step from names to language to affairs and onward.

lessons.title: The Junzi and the Small Man
lessons.mainIdea: Analects 4.16 contrasts the junzi, who thinks of what is right, with the small man, who thinks of gain.
reading: Analects 4.16 is a pair in one line. Legge: "The mind of the superior man is conversant with righteousness; the mind of the mean man is conversant with gain." "Conversant with" means familiar with, or thinking about. The Chinese for "mean man" is *xiaoren*, literally "small person."

The word for righteousness is *yi*: what is right or fitting to do. Many sayings in the Analects contrast the junzi and the xiaoren. The contrast is not about wealth or birth. It is about what a person's mind turns to first. A poor person can be a junzi, as Yan Hui was.

Readers argue about how firm the line is. Some take it as two kinds of people. Others read it as two directions any person can face. The Analects never says profit is always wrong. Other passages say wealth gained rightly is fine. The point of 4.16 is what comes first.

words.d: righteousness; what is right or fitting to do
"small person"; in the Analects, one whose mind turns first to gain; Legge writes "mean man"
a person of noble character; Legge writes "the superior man"

look.title: Righteousness and Gain
look.text: The mind of the superior man is conversant with righteousness; the mind of the mean man is conversant with gain.
look.cite: Confucian Analects 4.16, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1893
look.prompt: Is this saying about two kinds of people, or two choices anyone can make? Point to words that support your view.

check.q: According to Analects 4.16, what is the mind of the junzi familiar with?
check.why: Legge: "The mind of the superior man is conversant with righteousness."

check.q: What does xiaoren literally mean?
check.why: Xiaoren is "small person," Legge's "mean man."

check.q: What does the lesson say the junzi-xiaoren contrast is about?
choices: Which city a person lives in
What a person's mind turns to first
check.why: The contrast concerns righteousness versus gain, not birth or wealth.

lessons.title: Reading a Saying With Its Neighbors
lessons.mainIdea: Sayings in the Analects often sit in small groups, and reading nearby chapters can change what one line seems to mean.
reading: Analects 4.15, the one thread, sits right before 4.16, the junzi and gain. Book 4 as a whole returns again and again to ren and the junzi. Many scholars think editors grouped sayings by theme. Reading one line alone, cut off from its neighbors, can miss that theme.

Here is a close-reading method. First, read the saying. Second, read two chapters before and after it. Third, note shared words, like ren, junzi or shu. Fourth, ask how the neighbors change or support your first reading. This is reading in *context*: the words and setting around a passage.

Context can also mean history. Confucius lived in a time of warring states and failing rulers. Many readers think this is why 13.3 cares so much about titles that no longer fit. Other readers stress that the sayings speak beyond their time. Both kinds of context help a reader avoid a quote pulled loose.

words.d: the words, passages and history around a text that help explain it
an idea that comes up again and again in a text
careful, slow reading that pays attention to each word and its setting

look.title: Neighbors in Book 4
look.text: 4.15: the one thread is zhong and shu. 4.16: the junzi thinks of righteousness; the small man of gain. 4.17: when you see a worthy person, think of becoming like them; when you see an unworthy one, look within yourself.
look.prompt: What shared idea connects these three neighbors? How does 4.17 change how you read 4.16?

check.q: What does reading a saying "in context" mean?
choices: Reading it with its neighboring passages and history
Reading it as fast as you can
check.why: Context is the surrounding text and history that shape meaning.

check.q: Why do many scholars think the Analects' books have themes?
choices: Each book was written by a different sage
Editors seem to have grouped sayings by topic
Legge rearranged them all by theme
The books are in alphabetical order
check.why: Book 4, for example, keeps returning to ren and the junzi.

check.q: Which passage comes right before 4.16 on the junzi and gain?
check.why: Analects 4.15, Zeng Zi's one thread, sits just before 4.16.

lessons.title: Readers Across Asia
lessons.mainIdea: Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese readers, as well as Chinese readers, have studied and debated these same sayings for centuries.
reading: The Analects spread far beyond China. In Korea, Confucian learning shaped the Joseon dynasty's schools and exams. In Japan, scholars such as Ito Jinsai read the Analects closely and challenged older commentaries. In Vietnam, royal exams tested the classics for centuries.

These readers did not simply copy Chinese views. Ito Jinsai, for example, argued for going back to the Analects itself rather than relying on Zhu Xi's readings. Korean scholars debated human nature in long letters. Each place built its own *tradition* of reading: a line of teachers and books handed down.

Today the Analects is read in schools, homes and universities across East Asia and around the world. Some readers study it as philosophy. Some keep it as a family and cultural heritage. Some question parts of it. Close readers can meet all of these voices and describe them without ranking them.

words.d: a line of teachers, books and practices handed down over time
the Korean dynasty (1392–1897) that made Confucian learning central to its government
ideas and practices passed down from earlier generations

check.why: Each place built its own tradition of reading, and the course describes them without ranking.

review.why: In 15.23 the Master answers Zigong with "RECIPROCITY."

review.q: What does Analects 12.22 say ren is?
review.why: In Legge's 12.22 the Master tells Fan Chi ren "is to love all men."

review.why: 6.9 praises Hui's virtue with a single bamboo dish of rice.

review.q: What is the rectification of names?
choices: Giving each disciple a new name
Making words and titles match reality
review.why: Analects 13.3 says names must be correct so language fits the truth of things.

review.q: In Analects 4.16, the mind of the mean man is conversant with what?
review.why: Legge: "the mind of the mean man is conversant with gain."

review.q: Why does a close reader check neighboring chapters?
choices: Neighboring chapters always contradict each other
Nearby sayings often share a theme that shapes meaning
